why.correct: A joint is defined by two structures meeting and being held together, not by movement. Many joints barely move.
options: Correct. Any meeting point of bone with bone, cartilage or tooth is a joint.
This describes only freely movable joints. Skull sutures are joints too, and they do not move in an adult.
This describes a ligament, which can help hold a joint together but is not the joint itself.
This describes the cartilage on a bone end, one part found in some joints, not the joint itself.

why.correct: The radius and ulna are joined along their length by a sheet of fibers, the interosseous membrane. A fibrous joint where bones are held by a ligament or membrane is a syndesmosis.
options: Correct. A sheet of fibers joining two separated bones is a syndesmosis.
A suture joins the interlocking edges of skull bones with very short fibers, not two forearm bones by a long sheet.
A gomphosis holds a tooth in its socket.
A symphysis joins bones with a pad of fibrocartilage, not a sheet of fibers.

why.correct: The joint between a tooth root and its bony socket is a gomphosis, a fibrous joint held by the periodontal ligament.
options: A synchondrosis joins bones with hyaline cartilage, such as the epiphyseal plate. A tooth is held by fibers.
A syndesmosis joins two bones with a ligament or interosseous membrane, like the radius and ulna.
Correct. A tooth held in its socket by fibers is a gomphosis.
A suture joins two skull bones along a wavy seam.

why.correct: The periodontal ligament is the thin layer of collagen fibers running from the tooth root to the socket wall. It forms the gomphosis.
options: An interosseous membrane is the broad sheet of fibers between two long bones, such as the radius and ulna.
Correct. The fibers around the tooth root are the periodontal ligament.
Articular cartilage is hyaline cartilage covering bone ends, not fibers around a tooth root.
The periosteum is the membrane covering the outer surface of a bone, not the fibers tying a tooth to its socket.

why.correct: The pad of fibrocartilage joining the two pubic bones at the front of the pelvis is the pubic symphysis.
options: The sacrum is the bone at the back of the pelvis, not the joint at the front midline.
Correct. The fibrocartilage joint at the front midline of the pelvis is the pubic symphysis.
The acetabulum is the socket on the side of each hip bone that holds the head of the femur.
The epiphyseal plate is the hyaline cartilage joint inside a growing long bone.

why.correct: In a synovial joint the bone ends are separated by a narrow fluid-filled space, lined by a synovial membrane. Fibrous and cartilaginous joints are solid all the way across.
options: Synovial joints occur in the jaw and spine as well as the limbs, so location does not define them.
Joining bones by fibrocartilage describes a symphysis, a cartilaginous joint.
Correct. The fluid-filled space is the defining feature.
The contact surfaces of bone ends in a synovial joint are covered by cartilage, not periosteum.

why.correct: Sutures, gomphoses and syndesmoses are the three fibrous joints. The pubic symphysis and the epiphyseal plate are cartilaginous.
options: Yes. A suture is a fibrous joint between skull bones.
Yes. A tooth in its socket is a gomphosis, a fibrous joint.
Yes. Bones joined by an interosseous membrane form a syndesmosis, a fibrous joint.
No. The pubic symphysis joins bones with fibrocartilage, so it is cartilaginous.
No. The epiphyseal plate is hyaline cartilage, a synchondrosis.

why.correct: When growth in length stops, bone replaces the hyaline cartilage of the plate. A joint whose connecting tissue has been replaced by bone, fusing two bones into one, is a synostosis.
options: The plate was a synchondrosis while it was cartilage. Once bone replaces the cartilage, it no longer is.
A symphysis is joined by fibrocartilage, such as the pubic symphysis. The growth plate was never fibrocartilage.
Correct. The old growth plate is now bone, so it is a synostosis.
A syndesmosis joins two bones with a ligament or interosseous membrane. There is no ligament here.

why.correct: A fibrocartilage pad makes a symphysis, and slight movement makes it an amphiarthrosis. The intervertebral discs and the pubic symphysis fit this pair.
options: Correct. Fibrocartilage pad plus slight movement is a symphysis and an amphiarthrosis.
A synchondrosis uses hyaline cartilage and barely moves. This joint uses fibrocartilage and bends.
A suture is a fibrous joint between skull bones with no cartilage pad.
A syndesmosis is fibrous, not cartilaginous, and it is not freely movable.

why.correct: In pregnancy, hormones loosen the collagen in the fibrocartilage pad and ligaments of the pubic symphysis. The tissue stretches more under load, so the gap widens and the bones shift.
options: Bone formation would lock the joint and narrow the movement, not widen the gap. That would be a synostosis.
Correct. Looser collagen stretches more, and the joint gives more.
The joint's structural class does not change. It is still a fibrocartilage symphysis; only its tissue has become more stretchy.
The pubic symphysis has no fluid-filled space. It stays a solid fibrocartilage joint.

why.correct: A suture is a synarthrosis (immobile), the pubic symphysis is an amphiarthrosis (slightly movable), and the shoulder is a synovial diarthrosis (freely movable).
options: The sagittal suture's interlocking edges and short fibers allow almost no movement.
The pubic symphysis gives a little because its fibrocartilage pad bends.
The shoulder is a synovial joint that moves freely in many directions.

why.correct: A suture is an immobile joint, a synarthrosis. An intervertebral disc allows slight movement, so it is an amphiarthrosis.
options: Correct. The disc is slightly movable.
A diarthrosis is freely movable, like a synovial joint. One disc allows only slight movement.
A synostosis is a joint that has turned to bone. A healthy disc is fibrocartilage.
A syndesmosis is a structural subtype (a fibrous joint), not a functional class, and a disc is cartilaginous.

why.correct: The first rib's costal cartilage joins it to the manubrium with hyaline cartilage, making a synchondrosis, not a symphysis. A symphysis uses fibrocartilage.
options: Correct pairing. The coronal suture is a suture.
Correct pairing. A tooth in its socket is a gomphosis.
This is the wrong pairing. The first rib and manubrium are joined by hyaline cartilage, a synchondrosis.
Correct pairing. The interosseous membrane makes a syndesmosis.
Correct pairing. The pubic symphysis is joined by fibrocartilage.

why.correct: Sutures and gomphoses are immobile fibrous joints, while syndesmoses are slightly movable fibrous joints. One structural class spans two functional classes.
options: The joint between the sacrum and hip bone is synovial but held so tightly by ligaments that it barely moves, so it is close to an amphiarthrosis.
Synchondroses such as the epiphyseal plate are nearly immobile, so they are synarthroses, not amphiarthroses.
Correct. Fibrous joints span synarthroses and amphiarthroses.
The two schemes are separate. Structure predicts function most of the time, but that joint and the synchondroses show the groupings differ.

why.correct: In a newborn, the fibrous tissue between skull bones is wide, especially at the fontanelles, so the bones have room to shift. As the child grows, the bone edges come together and interlock.
options: Skull sutures are fibrous joints at every age. They never have a fluid-filled space.
Correct. Wide bands of fibrous tissue let the bones move slightly.
Skull bones are joined by fibrous tissue, not fibrocartilage.
A synostosis is fused bone, which would allow no movement at all. Most sutures fuse much later, if at all.

why.correct: Replacing a flexible fibrocartilage pad with bone turns an amphiarthrosis into a synostosis. Each level loses its small movement, and the lower back as a whole bends less.

variables.name: Movement between neighboring lumbar vertebrae
variables.why: Bone does not bend the way fibrocartilage does, so the vertebrae can no longer tilt or squeeze against each other.

variables.name: How many of these joints are synostoses
variables.why: Each disc replaced by bone fuses two vertebrae into one piece, which is the definition of a synostosis.

variables.name: How far the lower back can bend forward in total
variables.why: Bending of the whole spine is the sum of small movements at many discs. Each fused level adds nothing, so the total falls.

why.correct: In a suture, interlocking bone edges are bound by very short fibers. In a syndesmosis, the bones sit farther apart and are joined by a longer ligament or membrane, which can give a little.
options: Neither suture nor syndesmosis relies on hyaline cartilage; both are fibrous joints.
A fluid-filled space defines a synovial joint. A syndesmosis is solid fibrous tissue.
Correct. Longer fibers between more widely spaced bones allow more movement.
A fibrocartilage pad defines a symphysis, a cartilaginous joint.

why.correct: The smooth layer of hyaline cartilage capping each bone end inside a synovial joint is the articular cartilage.
options: Correct. This cap on the bone end is articular cartilage.
The synovial membrane lines the inside of the capsule, not the contact surfaces of the bones.
The fibrous membrane is the outer layer of the capsule, wrapped around the outside of the joint.
The periosteum covers the outer surface of the bone outside the joint, not the surfaces that meet.

why.correct: The narrow space between the cartilage-covered bone ends, filled with synovial fluid, is the joint cavity.
options: The medullary cavity is the hollow inside the shaft of a long bone, holding marrow.
A bursa is a separate sac of synovial fluid outside the joint, between tissues that slide over bone.
Correct. This is the joint cavity, filled with synovial fluid.
An articular disc is a solid pad of fibrocartilage, not a fluid-filled space.

why.correct: The outer layer of the articular capsule is the fibrous membrane, dense connective tissue that attaches to the periosteum of each bone and holds the bones together.
options: The synovial membrane is the inner layer of the capsule, lining the cavity.
Correct. The tough outer layer is the fibrous membrane.
Articular cartilage covers the bone ends inside the cavity, not the outside of the joint.
The endosteum lines the inner surfaces of bone, such as the medullary cavity.

why.correct: The synovial membrane lines the joint cavity. Fluid filters out of its small blood vessels, and its cells add the slippery molecules that make synovial fluid thick.
options: Articular cartilage is fed by synovial fluid; it does not make it.
The fibrous membrane is the tough outer layer that holds the bones together. It does not line the cavity.
Correct. The synovial membrane makes synovial fluid.
The periosteum covers bone outside the joint and has nothing to do with synovial fluid.

why.correct: Articular cartilage has no blood vessels. Loading squeezes fluid out and releasing draws fresh synovial fluid in, carrying nutrients to the chondrocytes. A joint that never moves or bears load loses that pumping, so the cartilage is poorly fed.
options: Chondrocytes are fed by fluid, not by nerve signals, and cartilage has no nerves.
Correct. Movement and loading pump nutrients into avascular cartilage.
The synovial membrane keeps making fluid. The problem is that the fluid is not pumped through the cartilage.
Articular cartilage has no blood vessels at all, so none can narrow.

why.correct: A bursa is a flattened sac of synovial membrane with a film of synovial fluid, placed where tissues slide over bone. A tendon sheath is a tube-shaped bursa around a tendon.
options: Yes. A bursa is a sac of synovial membrane with synovial fluid inside.
Yes. It sits between moving layers so they glide.
No. A pad of fibrocartilage inside a joint is an articular disc, not a bursa.
Yes. A tendon sheath is a bursa stretched into a sleeve around a tendon.
No. Bursae lie outside the joint cavity, between skin, tendon, muscle and bone.

why.correct: The sac between the skin and the front of the patella is the prepatellar bursa, a subcutaneous bursa (pre- = in front of).
options: Correct. The sac in front of the patella, under the skin, is the prepatellar bursa.
The suprapatellar bursa lies above the patella, behind the tendon from the thigh, not in front of the patella.
The joint cavity lies between the femur and the tibia, not in front of the patella.
The infrapatellar fat pad is a mass of fat behind the patellar ligament, not a fluid sac.

why.correct: A ball-and-socket joint is multiaxial: the round head can swing in every plane and turn in its cup. The shoulder and the hip are examples.
options: A hinge joint is uniaxial and swings in one plane only.
A condyloid joint is biaxial: it swings in two planes but cannot turn.
A saddle joint is biaxial, with a wide range, but it does not allow the free turning of a ball in a socket.
Correct. Ball-and-socket joints are multiaxial.

why.correct: A peg turning inside a ring is a pivot joint. It moves around one axis, the bone's long axis, so it is uniaxial. This is the atlantoaxial joint, which turns the head side to side.
options: Correct. Peg in a ring means pivot, and one axis means uniaxial.
A plane joint has flat surfaces that glide. The dens is a rounded peg in a ring.
A condyloid joint fits an oval surface into an oval hollow and does not turn. The atlas on the occipital condyles is condyloid, but that is a different joint.
A hinge swings a bone back and forth in one plane. The atlantoaxial joint turns the atlas around the dens instead.

why.correct: The joint between the trapezium and the first metacarpal is a saddle joint, biaxial with a wide range. The finger carpometacarpal joints are plane joints that only glide slightly.
options: The thumb does have only two phalanges, but the sweep happens at its base, at the carpometacarpal joint, so phalanx count does not explain it.
Correct. The saddle shape of the thumb's carpometacarpal joint allows the wide two-plane movement.
All synovial joints, including the thumb's, have articular cartilage.
The thumb's carpometacarpal joint is synovial. A symphysis would barely move.

why.correct: The ligament that crosses inside the knee from the front of the tibia up and back to the femur is the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL).
options: The posterior cruciate ligament runs from the back of the tibia up and forward, the other arm of the X.
The patellar ligament lies in front of the knee, from the patella to the tibial tuberosity.
Correct. This is the anterior cruciate ligament.
The fibular collateral ligament lies on the outer side of the knee, outside the capsule, running to the fibula.

why.correct: The C-shaped fibrocartilage pad on the inner (medial) tibial condyle is the medial meniscus.
options: The lateral meniscus sits on the outer tibial condyle.
Correct. This is the medial meniscus.
Articular cartilage is the thin hyaline layer on the bone surface. The meniscus is a thicker fibrocartilage pad resting on it.
The tibial collateral ligament runs down the inner side of the knee from femur to tibia, not across the top of the tibia.

why.correct: The anterior cruciate ligament stops the tibia from sliding forward under the femur. When it is torn, the tibia can be pulled forward too far.
options: The posterior cruciate ligament stops the tibia sliding backward, so its tear shows when the tibia is pushed back.
Correct. Excess forward slide of the tibia points to the anterior cruciate ligament.
The menisci deepen and cushion the tibial surfaces; they do not act as the main restraint on forward slide.
The patellar ligament carries the pull of the thigh muscles to the tibia and does not restrain forward slide.

why.correct: A blow to the outer side pushes the knee inward, stretching the inner side. The tibial collateral ligament braces the inner side and is attached to the medial meniscus, so the two are often injured together.
options: Correct. The inner ligament tears, and the medial meniscus attached to it is at risk.
The fibular collateral ligament is on the outer side. A blow from the outside compresses that side rather than stretching it.
The posterior cruciate ligament restrains backward slide of the tibia, not inward bending of the knee.
The patellar ligament is in front of the knee and is not stretched by a sideways blow.

why.correct: The glenoid cavity is small and shallow, the capsule is loose, and the rotator cuff tendons do most of the holding. The hip has a deep acetabulum and a thick capsule with strong ligaments.
options: The shoulder's capsule is loose, not thick. A thick capsule would make it more stable.
The glenohumeral joint has a labrum around its rim but no articular disc between the bones.
Correct. A shallow socket held mainly by muscles is easy to push out of place.
Both the shoulder and the hip are ball-and-socket joints.

why.correct: The ring of fibrocartilage around the rim of the glenoid cavity of the scapula is the glenoid labrum. It deepens the shallow shoulder socket.
options: The acetabular labrum rims the socket of the hip, not the shoulder.
An articular disc lies between two bone ends. The labrum is a rim around the socket's edge.
Correct. This is the glenoid labrum.
The subacromial bursa is a fluid sac above the joint, under the acromion.

why.correct: The head of the radius turns inside the annular ligament at the proximal radioulnar joint. A sharp pull slides it partly out while the surfaces still touch: a partial dislocation, or subluxation.
options: A sprain is a stretch or tear of a ligament. Here the bone has slipped out of the ligament's ring.
A dislocation separates the joint surfaces completely. Here they are only partly out of line, and the humeroulnar joint is not involved.
A fracture is a break in a bone. The X-rays are normal.
Correct. This is a subluxation of the radial head from the annular ligament.

why.correct: Cartilage damage comes first. As the cartilage thins, the gap between the bones narrows. Once it wears through, bone meets bone and spurs form, and pain and stiffness follow.
options: The disease begins with damage to the avascular cartilage, which repairs poorly.
Damaged cartilage loses its structure and thins.
Thinner cartilage fills less of the space between the bones, so the gap looks narrower.
Where cartilage is gone, bone rubs bone and reacts by thickening and forming spurs.
Bone-on-bone contact and irritation of the synovial membrane cause pain and stiffness.

why.correct: The distal tibiofibular joint is not synovial at all. The lower ends of the tibia and fibula are joined by strong ligaments, a syndesmosis.
options: Correct pairing. The atlas turns around the dens.
Correct pairing. The wrist joint is condyloid.
Correct pairing. The joints between the finger bones are hinges.
This is the wrong pairing. The distal tibiofibular joint is a fibrous syndesmosis.
Correct pairing. The sternoclavicular joint is a saddle joint with an articular disc.

why.correct: Rolling the sole inward stretches the outer side of the ankle, where the ligaments are smaller and weaker. The anterior talofibular ligament gives first. A stretched or torn ligament is a sprain.
options: Correct. The anterior talofibular ligament is the one most often sprained.
The deltoid ligament is on the inner side and is compressed, not stretched, when the sole rolls inward. It is also very strong.
The ligament is right, but a dislocation means the bone surfaces are forced fully apart, which is not described.
The iliofemoral ligament is at the hip, not the ankle.

why.correct: The fibular collateral ligament runs from the femur to the head of the fibula outside the capsule, so it is an extrinsic ligament.
options: Correct. It is an extrinsic ligament.
The anterior cruciate ligament is intracapsular: inside the capsule, covered by synovial membrane.
The tibial collateral ligament is part of the capsule's fibrous membrane, so it is intrinsic.
The posterior cruciate ligament is intracapsular, like the anterior one.

why.correct: Losing the anterior cruciate ligament removes the restraint on forward slide of the tibia. The unstable knee grinds its menisci and cartilage when it pivots, but restraints handled by other ligaments stay the same.

variables.name: How far the tibia can slide forward under the femur
variables.why: The anterior cruciate ligament is the main restraint on forward slide of the tibia, so with it torn the tibia slides farther.

variables.name: Shear forces on the menisci during pivoting
variables.why: When the tibia shifts and twists abnormally, the femur grinds across the menisci and shears them.

variables.name: How far the tibia can slide backward under the femur
variables.why: Backward slide of the tibia is restrained mainly by the posterior cruciate ligament, which is intact, so this does not change.

why.correct: Flexion is a sagittal-plane movement that makes the angle between two bones smaller, such as bending the elbow.
options: Abduction moves a limb away from the midline in the frontal plane.
Extension is the opposite of flexion: it makes the angle larger again.
Correct. Flexion decreases the angle.
Rotation turns a bone around its own long axis in the transverse plane.

why.correct: The hand traces a circle while the shoulder stays put, so the arm sweeps out a cone. That is circumduction.
options: Rotation turns the bone around its own long axis; it does not trace a circle with the limb's end.
Correct. Tracing a circle with the end of the limb is circumduction.
Abduction lifts the arm out to the side in one direction only.
Opposition is a thumb movement that brings the thumb tip to a fingertip.

why.correct: The arm moves out to the side, away from the midline, in the frontal plane. That is abduction.
options: Adduction brings the arm back toward the midline, the return movement.
Flexion at the shoulder lifts the arm forward in the sagittal plane, not out to the side.
Correct. Moving the arm away from the midline is abduction.
Elevation moves a bone such as the scapula or mandible upward; it is not the name for lifting the arm sideways.

why.correct: The thigh turns on its long axis so that its front faces away from the midline. That is lateral rotation.
options: Correct. The front of the limb turns outward.
Medial rotation turns the front of the limb toward the midline, the opposite way.
Circumduction sweeps the limb in a cone; here the thigh only turns on its axis.
Abduction moves the whole limb away from the midline; it does not turn the limb on its long axis.

why.correct: Lifting the top of the foot toward the shin is dorsiflexion.
options: Plantar flexion points the foot down, the opposite movement.
Inversion turns the sole inward; it does not lift the foot toward the shin.
Correct. The top of the foot moves toward the shin.
Eversion turns the sole outward.

why.correct: The sole of the foot turns outward, away from the midline. That is eversion.
options: Inversion turns the sole inward, toward the other foot.
Correct. The sole faces outward.
Dorsiflexion lifts the top of the foot toward the shin; the sole does not turn.
The foot's sideways turning of the sole has its own name; abduction is used for limbs moving away from the midline.

why.correct: Jutting the lower jaw forward is protraction of the mandible.
options: Elevation raises the mandible to close the mouth.
Lateral excursion slides the jaw to one side.
Correct. Moving the jaw forward is protraction.
Depression lowers the mandible to open the mouth.

why.correct: In anatomical position the palms face forward and the radius and ulna lie parallel. That is the supinated position.
options: Correct. Anatomical position has the forearm supinated.
In the pronated position the palm faces backward and the radius crosses the ulna.
The elbow is straight in anatomical position, not flexed.
Hyperextension is extension past anatomical position, so anatomical position cannot be hyperextended.

why.correct: The angle between the thigh and the leg gets smaller, so this is flexion. At the knee, flexion carries the leg backward.
options: The leg does move backward, but direction of travel does not name the movement. The angle decreases, so it is flexion, not extension.
Correct. Flexion is defined by the angle getting smaller.
The leg does pass behind the body, but hyperextension is extension past anatomical position. The knee is bending, not straightening.
Adduction is a frontal-plane movement toward the midline. The heel moves backward in the sagittal plane.

why.correct: Turning the palm up (forward, in anatomical terms) is supination: the radius swings back to lie parallel with the ulna.
options: Pronation turns the palm down or backward, the opposite way.
Correct. Palm up is supination.
Dorsiflexion is a movement of the foot at the ankle.
Lateral excursion is sideways movement of the mandible.

why.correct: In pronation the head of the radius turns in the annular ligament at the proximal radioulnar joint, and the lower end of the radius swings around the ulna at the distal radioulnar joint. The hand goes along with the radius.
options: The radiocarpal joint is the wrist. The wrist does not turn the palm; the hand simply rides on the radius.
The humeroulnar joint is the elbow's hinge. It bends and straightens the elbow but cannot turn the forearm.
Correct. Pronation happens between the radius and the ulna.
The midcarpal joint lies between the two rows of carpal bones and only glides.

why.correct: The head moved backward beyond anatomical position in the sagittal plane: hyperextension. It stretches the structures on the front of the neck.
options: Hyperflexion is flexion beyond the normal range, bending the head forward.
Lateral flexion tilts the head toward a shoulder, in the frontal plane.
Rotation turns the head side to side around the axis of the neck.
Correct. The head went backward past upright: hyperextension.

why.correct: The frontal plane divides front from back, so movements in it carry parts out to the side or back to the midline: abduction, adduction and lateral flexion.
options: Yes. Lifting the arm out to the side is a frontal-plane movement.
Yes. Bending the trunk to the side is a frontal-plane movement.
No. Elbow flexion happens in the sagittal plane.
Yes. Bringing the thigh toward the midline is a frontal-plane movement.
No. Rotation turns a bone around its long axis in the transverse plane.

why.correct: Circumduction strings together movement in two planes: flexion, abduction, extension and adduction. A hinge joint moves in one plane only, so it cannot circumduct.
options: A condyloid joint moves in two planes, so it can circumduct (the wrist, the knuckles).
A saddle joint moves in two planes, so it can circumduct (the base of the thumb).
A ball-and-socket joint moves in every plane and circumducts easily (the shoulder, the hip).
Correct. A hinge moves in one plane and cannot sweep a cone.

why.correct: Moving a bone straight up is elevation. Shrugging elevates the scapulae.
options: Protraction moves the scapulae forward around the rib cage, as when you reach forward.
Superior rotation turns the scapula so the glenoid cavity tips up, as when the arm is raised overhead. A shrug lifts the whole scapula without turning it.
Correct. Shrugging is elevation.
Abduction describes a limb moving away from the midline, not the scapula moving up.

why.correct: Circumduction is the four angular movements in sequence. Starting forward: flexion lifts the arm forward, abduction carries it out to the side, extension swings it back, and adduction returns it to your side.
options: The arm first rises forward: flexion.
It then swings out to the side: abduction.
It then moves back behind the side: extension.
It finally returns to the side of the body: adduction.

why.correct: Dorsiflexion and plantar flexion are an opposite pair at the ankle. Inversion's opposite is eversion: turning the sole outward instead of inward.
options: Correct. Eversion is the opposite of inversion.
Pronation is the forearm movement that turns the palm backward, the opposite of supination.
Abduction is the opposite of adduction.
Depression is the opposite of elevation.

why.correct: Bringing the thumb tip across the palm to a fingertip is opposition. It happens mainly at the saddle-shaped carpometacarpal joint at the base of the thumb.
options: Correct. Opposition at the thumb's saddle joint.
The thumb's interphalangeal joint is a hinge that only bends the tip; it cannot carry the thumb across the palm.
Flexion at the wrist bends the whole hand forward; it does not bring the thumb to a finger.
Reposition is the return of the thumb to its resting place, the opposite movement.

why.correct: Plantar flexion points the foot down at the talocrural (ankle) joint. The radiocarpal joint is the wrist.
options: Correct pairing. The radius turns around the ulna at the radioulnar joints.
Correct pairing. Turning the sole inward happens mostly at the subtalar joint.
Correct pairing. The jaw slides sideways at the temporomandibular joint.
This is the wrong pairing. Plantar flexion happens at the ankle, not the wrist.
Correct pairing. Shaking the head "no" happens at the atlantoaxial pivot joint.

why.correct: Elbow flexion closes the elbow angle, and pronation crosses the radius over the ulna. The wrist takes no part in either.

variables.name: Angle between the upper arm and the forearm
variables.why: Flexion at the elbow decreases the angle between the humerus and the forearm bones.

variables.name: How much the radius crosses over the ulna
variables.why: In anatomical position the radius and ulna are parallel. Pronation swings the radius across the ulna.

variables.name: Angle at the wrist between the forearm and the hand
variables.why: Neither movement happens at the wrist. The hand rides along with the radius during pronation, so the wrist angle does not change.

why.correct: Raising the arm high overhead needs the scapula to turn so that its glenoid cavity tips upward: superior rotation. If the scapula does not rotate, the arm stops a little past shoulder height even with a healthy shoulder joint.
options: Correct. Without superior rotation of the scapula the arm cannot go high overhead.
Medial rotation of the humerus turns the arm inward on its axis; it does not raise it overhead.
Depression lowers the scapula, which would not help lift the arm.
Lateral flexion of the neck tilts the head and does not lift the arm.
